plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 14.3.3
plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a polar rectangle R, the fundamental building block for polar double integration. The region R is bounded by two circular arcs r = 1.5 and r = 2 (solid blue curves) and two rays theta = pi/6 and theta = pi/4 (dashed red lines), forming a curved quadrilateral shaded in light blue and labeled R. The figure introduces the polar rectangle as the analogue of the Cartesian rectangle for setting up double integrals in polar coordinates, showing how its curved sides arise from the constant-r and constant-theta boundary conditions.

interactionPlan.concept: A polar rectangle R is the region swept between two constant-radius arcs and two constant-angle rays, and it is the natural building block for double integration in polar coordinates.
elements: Horizontal black baseline representing the polar axis (positive x-axis), with the pole/origin at its left end
Dashed red ray from the origin at angle theta = pi/6 (lower bounding ray), extending past the outer arc
Dashed red ray from the origin at angle theta = pi/4 (upper bounding ray), extending past the outer arc
Solid blue circular arc of radius r = 1.5 (inner arc), drawn over an angular span wider than the region so its ends stick out past both rays
Solid blue circular arc of radius r = 2 (outer arc), drawn similarly over-extended
Light-blue shaded curved quadrilateral R bounded by the two arcs and two rays
Label 'r = 1.5' with leader pointing to the inner arc
Label 'r = 2' with leader pointing to the outer arc
Label 'theta = pi/6' placed below/right along the lower dashed ray
Label 'theta = pi/4' placed left along the upper dashed ray
Italic label 'R' centered inside the shaded region
Optional overlay: dashed grey straight-sided rectangle of dimensions delta-r by r*delta-theta anchored at the inner-lower corner of R
Optional overlay annotations: delta-r radial thickness bracket, r*delta-theta arc-length bracket, and area expression
Faint polar grid of concentric circles and radial spokes for context

interactions.teaches: The inner boundary of a polar rectangle is a curve of constant r, so moving it slides a circular arc rather than a straight line.
interactions.label: Inner radius r₁

interactions.teaches: Δr = r₂ − r₁ controls the radial thickness of R; as r₂ → r₁ the region collapses to an arc.
interactions.label: Outer radius r₂

interactions.teaches: Holding r fixed and rotating the lower ray sweeps R around the pole without changing its radial extent.
interactions.label: Start angle θ₁ (× π)

interactions.teaches: Δθ = θ₂ − θ₁ controls the angular width; the outer edge grows faster than the inner edge because arc length is r·Δθ.
interactions.label: End angle θ₂ (× π)

interactions.teaches: R is only an analogue of a rectangle: a true Δr × rΔθ rectangle matches it at a corner but its straight sides peel away from the circular arcs, and the mismatch shrinks as R shrinks.
interactions.label: Overlay straight Δr × rΔθ rectangle

demo_steps.title: The region as drawn
demo_steps.narration: The shaded region R is trapped between the circular arcs r = 1.5 and r = 2 and the rays θ = π/6 and θ = π/4. Its four sides come from just two equations: r = constant and θ = constant.

demo_steps.title: Change the radial bounds
demo_steps.narration: Push the arcs apart while keeping the rays fixed. R grows only in the radial direction — the curved sides slide outward but the straight sides stay on the same two rays.

demo_steps.title: Change the angular bounds
demo_steps.narration: Now fix the radii and open the rays. R sweeps through a wider wedge, and notice the outer edge lengthens more than the inner edge — arc length is r·Δθ, so it depends on how far out you are.

demo_steps.title: Compare with a true rectangle
demo_steps.narration: Overlay a straight-sided rectangle of the same Δr by rΔθ dimensions at the inner corner. Its flat sides visibly miss the arcs — R is curved, not a real rectangle.

demo_steps.title: Shrink it toward a differential element
demo_steps.narration: Make Δr and Δθ small. The straight rectangle and the curved region become indistinguishable, which is exactly why dA = r dr dθ works inside a double integral.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A polar rectangle isn't a rectangle — two of its sides are arcs of length r·Δθ — but as Δr and Δθ shrink it behaves like a Δr by rΔθ rectangle, which is where the factor r in dA = r dr dθ comes from.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Pole at the lower-left, horizontal black polar axis running right. Two thin dashed red rays leave the pole at the two angles and extend well past the outer arc. Two thick solid blue circular arcs centered at the pole, drawn a bit wider than the angular span so their ends visibly overrun the rays (as in the original). The enclosed curved quadrilateral is filled pale blue with a bold italic serif 'R' at its centroid. Labels in serif math style: 'r = 1.5' and 'r = 2' to the upper-left of each arc with short leader lines, 'θ = π/6' below the lower ray and 'θ = π/4' to the left of the upper ray, both with stacked fractions. Labels should update live to the slider values (show θ as a multiple of π). When the overlay toggle is on, draw a grey dashed straight-sided rectangle anchored at the inner-lower corner of R, width Δr along the θ₁ direction and height r₁·Δθ perpendicular to it, with small bracket annotations 'Δr' and 'r Δθ' and a caption 'area ≈ r Δr Δθ'. Keep a very faint polar grid (concentric circles at integer radii, spokes every π/12) behind everything for orientation.

plan.authoredInteractions:

Polar rectangle R

Hover or click the arcs, rays and shaded region for explanations.

discrepancies: Scale/composition: the polar rectangle is drawn at roughly half the relative size of the source (S=132 with arcs at r≈1.5–2 inside a 700×520 viewbox), leaving a large empty region above and to the right; in the source the arcs and wedge fill most of the frame.
A faint grey polar grid (three concentric arcs plus seven radial spokes) is added that does not exist in the source figure, adding clutter behind the wedge.

Label layout differs: 'r = 2' and 'r = 1.5' are pushed into a tight left-hand column with grey leader lines that cross the red dashed rays, and 'r = 1.5' sits immediately above 'θ = π/4', producing crowding that the airy source layout avoids.
Label size relative to the artwork is smaller than the source, where 'r = 2', 'θ = π/4' etc. are large, prominent serif annotations; here they read as small marginal text next to the shrunken wedge.
The black baseline axis extends past the left of the pole (OX−12) and to the far right edge; in the source it starts essentially at the pole and is a simple horizontal rule.
evaluation.notes: Correct primitives (thick blue arcs, dashed red rays, pale blue shaded R, baseline axis) and an excellent, conceptually deep interaction set (four sliders, Δr×rΔθ overlay, five-step narrated player, live area readout), but the wedge is drawn at about half the source's relative scale inside a mostly empty canvas, an invented grey polar grid adds clutter, and the r-labels crowd the θ-labels with leaders crossing the rays.
action_items: Increase the drawing scale (larger S and/or tighter viewbox) so the r=1.5–2 wedge fills the frame like the source, reducing the empty area at top-right; optionally auto-fit S to the current r₂.
Remove or drastically lighten the invented concentric grid arcs and radial spokes so the default state matches the clean source composition.

Re-place 'r = 2' and 'r = 1.5' up and to the left of their arc ends (as in the source) with short leaders that do not cross the dashed rays, and add vertical separation from the 'θ = π/4' label to avoid crowding.
Trim the baseline axis so it begins at the pole rather than extending 12px to its left, and scale annotation font sizes up with the enlarged figure for inline legibility.

feedback.rationale: Concept and interaction structure are sound (concept 5, no plan action items); the issues are purely implementation-level—drawing scale, an invented grid, label placement, and axis extent—which are concrete rendering fixes.

discrepancies: The wedge occupies a smaller share of the frame than in the source: the pole sits at the far lower-left but the arcs/region are drawn noticeably smaller, leaving more empty space above and right of the region than the original.
The generated figure adds thin grey leader lines from the 'r = 2' and 'r = 1.5' labels to the arc ends; the source places the labels directly adjacent to the arc tips with no connectors.
Arc overrun past the rays is shorter and more symmetric than the source, where the r = 2 arc in particular extends conspicuously far beyond both bounding rays.

The dashed red rays in the generated version use a longer dash pattern and slightly thinner stroke than the source's dashes, and the 'R' glyph is rendered bold whereas the source uses a plain italic serif R.
evaluation.notes: A near drop-in replacement for the source polar-rectangle figure — correct arcs, dashed rays, shaded region, colors and stacked-fraction θ labels — backed by four meaningful sliders, an overlay toggle, a five-step narrated demo and a correct area readout; only minor cosmetic deviations (smaller wedge in frame, added leader lines, bold R) hold it back.
action_items: Increase the auto-fit scale (or reduce the reserved margins) so the wedge fills the canvas at the default state as tightly as in the source.
Drop the grey leader lines and place 'r = 2' / 'r = 1.5' directly at the upper ends of their arcs, as in the original.
Render the region label R in plain italic serif (not bold) and lengthen the arc overrun past the rays to match the source's generous overhang.
Verify at extreme slider values (very small Δθ, r₁ near r₂) that the two θ fraction labels and the 'area ≈ r Δr Δθ' overlay text do not collide with the rays, the axis line, or each other.

feedback.rationale: No failure modes, all core scores at or near 5, and the remaining action items are minor cosmetic polish rather than conceptual or structural defects.
